claim: In South Africa alone, over 12,000 wildlife road mortality incidents were recorded by The Endangered Wildlife Trust's 'Wildlife and Roads Project' from 1949 to 2017.
source: In South Africa alone, over 12,000 wildlife road mortality incidents were recorded by The Endangered Wildlife Trust's "Wildlife and Roads Project" from 1949 to 2017 (Endangered Wildlife Trust 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the Endangered Wildlife Trust 2017 report.

claim: The bat-eared fox (Otocyon megalotis) and the aardwolf (Proteles cristatus) are among the most frequently encountered mammalian roadkill species in South Africa.
source: Here, we studied two of the most frequently encountered mammalian roadkill species in South Africa (Périquet et al., 2018): the bat-eared fox (Otocyon megalotis, Canidae) and the aardwolf (Proteles cristatus, Hyaenidae).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Périquet et al., 2018.

claim: The bat-eared fox is divided into the Southern bat-eared fox (O. megalotis megalotis) and the Eastern bat-eared fox (O. megalotis virgatus).
source: The bat-eared fox is divided into the Southern bat-eared fox (O. megalotis megalotis) and the Eastern bat-eared fox (O. megalotis virgatus) (Clark, 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Clark, 2005.

claim: No genetic or genomic assessment of population differentiation has been conducted for the bat-eared fox and aardwolf subspecies to date.
source: However, despite known differences in behaviour between the subspecies of both species groups (Wilson et al., 2009), no genetic or genomic assessment of population differentiation has been conducted to date.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text with a citation to Wilson et al., 2009 for behavioral differences.

claim: 27.3 Gb of raw Nanopore long reads were sequenced using 16 MinION flow cells for the Southern aardwolf (P. c. cristatus).
source: In total, after high-accuracy basecalling, adapter trimming, and quality filtering, 27.3 Gb of raw Nanopore long reads were sequenced using 16 MinION flow cells for the Southern aardwolf (P. c. cristatus)
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by sequencing data presented in Table 1.

claim: 33.0 Gb of raw Nanopore long reads were sequenced using 13 MinION flow cells for the Southern bat-eared fox (O. m. megalotis).
source: In total, after high-accuracy basecalling, adapter trimming, and quality filtering, 27.3 Gb of raw Nanopore long reads were sequenced using 16 MinION flow cells for the Southern aardwolf (P. c. cristatus) and 33.0 Gb using 13 flow cells for the Southern bat-eared fox (O. m. megalotis) (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by sequencing data presented in Table 1.

claim: The N50 of the DNA fragment size for P. cristatus (9,175 bp) was about two times higher than the N50 of the DNA fragment size obtained for O. megalotis (4,393 bp).
source: Owing to quality differences among the extracted tissues for both species, the N50 of the DNA fragment size for P. cristatus (9,175 bp) was about two times higher than the N50 of the DNA fragment size obtained for O. megalotis (4,393 bp).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by sequencing data presented in Table 1.

claim: The hybrid assembly for the aardwolf (P. cristatus) resulted in 5,669 scaffolds with an N50 of 1.3 Mb.
source: Hybrid assemblies for both species were obtained with a high degree of contiguity with only 5,669 scaffolds and an N50 of 1.3 Mb for the aardwolf (P. cristatus)
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by assembly statistics in Table 1.

claim: The hybrid assembly for the bat-eared fox (O. megalotis) resulted in 11,081 scaffolds with an N50 of 728 kb.
source: Hybrid assemblies for both species were obtained with a high degree of contiguity with only 5,669 scaffolds and an N50 of 1.3 Mb for the aardwolf (P. cristatus) and 11,081 scaffolds and an N50 of 728 kb for the bat-eared fox (O. megalotis) (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by assembly statistics in Table 1.

claim: The two new genomes showed high BUSCO scores indicating high completeness.
source: Our two new genomes compared favorably with the available carnivoran genome assemblies in terms of (i) contiguity showing slightly less than the median N50 and a lower number of scaffolds than the majority of the other assemblies (Appendix 1—figure 2, Supplementary file 3) and (ii) completeness showing high BUSCO scores (see Appendix 1—figure 3 and Supplementary file 4 for BUSCO score comparisons among carnivoran genomes).
evidence: The claim is supported by BUSCO analysis data and comparison with other carnivoran genomes, as shown in Appendix 1—figure 3 and Supplementary file 4.

claim: The patristic distances between the allopatric subspecies of aardwolf and bat-eared fox were 0.045 and 0.020 substitutions per site, respectively.
source: The patristic distances, extracted from the phylogenetic tree inferred with complete mitogenomes between the allopatric subspecies of aardwolf and bat-eared fox, were 0.045 and 0.020 substitutions per site, respectively (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by phylogenetic analysis data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The genetic distance between the two subspecies of aardwolf (0.045 substitutions per site) is comparable to that observed between the red fox (Vulpes vulpes) and the fennec (V. zerda) (0.029).
source: These genetic distances are comparable to those observed between different well-defined species of Carnivora, such as the red fox (Vulpes vulpes) and the fennec (V. zerda) (0.029) or the steppe polecat (Mustela eversmanii) and the Siberian weasel (M. sibirica) (0.034) (see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by comparative phylogenetic distance data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: A threshold between polymorphism and divergence of approximately 0.02 substitutions per site was identified for Carnivora based on COX1 and CYTB genes.
source: Despite an overlap between polymorphism and divergence in both mitochondrial genes, this analysis revealed a threshold between polymorphism and divergence of approximately 0.02 substitutions per site for Carnivora (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by analysis of COX1 and CYTB sequence data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The genetic distance between the two subspecies of aardwolf (Proteles ssp.) was 0.054 for both COX1 and CYTB, which is higher than the majority of intraspecific distances observed across Carnivora.
source: With a patristic distance of 0.054 for both COX1 and CYTB, the genetic distance observed between the two subspecies of aardwolf (Proteles ssp.) was higher than the majority of the intraspecific distances observed across Carnivora.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by comparative analysis of mitochondrial gene sequences.

claim: The genetic distances between the two subspecies of bat-eared fox (Otocyon ssp.) were 0.020 for COX1 and 0.032 for CYTB, which fall in an ambiguous zone.
source: However, with patristic distances of 0.020 for COX1 and 0.032 for CYTB, the genetic distances observed between the two subspecies of bat-eared fox (Otocyon ssp.) were clearly in the ambiguous zone and did not provide a clear indication of the specific taxonomic status of these populations.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by comparative analysis of mitochondrial gene sequences.

claim: The mean heterozygosity was 0.189 per kb in the Southern aardwolf population and 0.121 per kb in the Eastern aardwolf population.
source: For the aardwolf, the mean heterozygosity was 0.189 per kb (sd = 0.010) in the Southern population and 0.121 per kb (sd = 0.008) in the Eastern population.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by genome-wide heterozygosity analysis.

claim: The mean heterozygosity was 0.209 per kb in the Southern bat-eared fox population and 0.127 per kb in the Eastern bat-eared fox population.
source: For the bat-eared fox, the mean heterozygosity was 0.209 per kb (sd = 0.013) in the Southern population and 0.127 per kb (sd = 0.003) in the Eastern population.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by genome-wide heterozygosity analysis.

claim: The heterozygosity level in aardwolf and bat-eared fox is low compared to other large mammals and is comparable to that of the Iberian lynx, cheetah, or brown hyaena.
source: This heterozygosity level is low compared to that of other large mammals (Díez-Del-Molino et al., 2018) and is comparable to that of the Iberian lynx, the cheetah or the brown hyaena, which have notoriously low genetic diversity (Abascal et al., 2016; Casas-Marce et al., 2013; Westbury et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to comparative studies on genetic diversity in large mammals.

claim: The genetic differentiation index (GDI) between the two subspecies of aardwolf was 0.533.
source: In contrast, the genetic differentiation estimates for the two pairs of individuals belonging to the different subspecies were respectively equal on average to 0.533 and 0.294 for P. cristatus ssp. and O. megalotis ssp.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by genome-wide GDI analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The genetic differentiation index (GDI) between the two subspecies of bat-eared fox was 0.294.
source: In contrast, the genetic differentiation estimates for the two pairs of individuals belonging to the different subspecies were respectively equal on average to 0.533 and 0.294 for P. cristatus ssp. and O. megalotis ssp.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by genome-wide GDI analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The genetic differentiation between the two subspecies of aardwolf (GDI = 0.533) is higher than that between the gray wolf (C. lupus) and the golden jackal (C. aureus) (GDI = 0.44).
source: The genetic differentiation indexes between the gray wolf (C. lupus) and the golden jackal (C. aureus) averaged 0.44, indicating that the two subspecies of aardwolf (GDI = 0.533) are genetically more differentiated than these two well-defined species
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by comparative GDI analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The genetic differentiation between the bat-eared fox subspecies (GDI = 0.294) was lower than the genetic differentiation estimates obtained for any of the four reference species pairs evaluated.
source: Conversely, the genetic differentiation obtained between the bat-eared fox subspecies (GDI = 0.294) was lower than the genetic differentiation estimates obtained for any of the four reference species pairs evaluated here (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by comparative GDI analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The two subspecies of P. cristatus warrant separate species status (P. cristatus and P. septentrionalis).
source: Our results, based on both mitochondrial and nuclear genome analyses, indicate that the two subspecies of aardwolf warrant elevation to species level (P. cristatus and P. septentrionalis)
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by multiple lines of genomic evidence including mitochondrial distances, GDI analysis, and comparative species delineation.

claim: The O. megalotis subspecies do not warrant elevation to species status.
source: Our results, based on both mitochondrial and nuclear genome analyses, indicate that the two subspecies of aardwolf warrant elevation to species level (P. cristatus and P. septentrionalis), but the O. megalotis subspecies do not warrant this status.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by multiple lines of genomic evidence including mitochondrial distances, GDI analysis, and comparative species delineation.

claim: The Eastern African populations of both aardwolf and bat-eared fox showed a continuous decrease in effective population size (Ne) over time.
source: For both the aardwolf and the bat-eared fox, the individual from Eastern African populations showed a continuous decrease in Ne over time, leading to the recent Ne being lower than that in Southern African populations (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by PSMC analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The trajectories of the three sampled bat-eared fox individuals synchronized approximately 200 kya ago, which could correspond to the time of divergence between the Southern and Eastern populations.
source: For the bat-eared fox, the trajectories of the three sampled individuals were synchronized approximately 200 kya ago (Figure 4a), which could correspond to the time of divergence between the Southern and Eastern populations.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by PSMC analysis shown in Figure 4a. The interpretation is speculative.

claim: The Southern populations of both aardwolf and bat-eared fox showed a marked increase in population size between ~10 and 30 kya before sharply decreasing in more recent times.
source: Interestingly, the Southern populations of both species showed a marked increase in population size between ~10 and 30 kya before sharply decreasing in more recent times (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by PSMC analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The phylogenomic dataset comprised 52 carnivoran species representing all but two families of the Carnivora (Nandiniidae and Prionodontidae).
source: Phylogenetic relationships within the Carnivora were inferred from a phylogenomic dataset comprising 52 carnivoran species (including the likely new Proteles septentrionalis species), representing all but two families of the Carnivora (Nandiniidae and Prionodontidae).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by the phylogenomic analysis.

claim: The supermatrix consisted of 14,307 genes representing a total of 24,041,987 nucleotide sites with 6,495,611 distinct patterns (27.0%) and 22.8% gaps or undetermined nucleotides.
source: These gene sets were used to create a supermatrix consisting of 14,307 genes representing a total of 24,041,987 nucleotide sites with 6,495,611 distinct patterns (27.0%) and 22.8% gaps or undetermined nucleotides.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by the phylogenomic dataset construction.

claim: The order Carnivora is divided into two distinct suborders: Feliformia (cat-related clade) and Caniformia (dog-related clade).
source: The order Carnivora was divided into two distinct suborders: a cat-related clade (Feliformia) and a dog-related clade (Caniformia).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Within the Hyaenidae, the two species of termite-eating aardwolves (P. cristatus and P. septentrionalis) were the sister-group of a clade composed of the carnivorous spotted (Crocuta crocuta) and striped (Hyaena hyaena) hyaenas.
source: In hyaenids, the two species of termite-eating aardwolves (P. cristatus and P. septentrionalis) were the sister-group of a clade composed of the carnivorous spotted (Crocuta crocuta) and striped (Hyaena hyaena) hyaenas.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The ML phylogenetic inference on the concatenation provided support for grouping the Pinnipedia and the Musteloidea to the exclusion of the Ursidae (bears) with maximum bootstrap support.
source: Within the Arctoidea, the ML phylogenetic inference on the concatenation provided support for grouping the Pinnipedia and the Musteloidea to the exclusion of the Ursidae (bears) with maximum bootstrap support (Figure 5)
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The concordance factor analyses revealed that many sites and many genes supported alternative topological conformations for the node grouping Pinnipedia and Musteloidea.
source: However, the concordance factor analyses revealed that many sites and many genes actually supported alternative topological conformations for this node characterized by a very short branch length (sCF = 34.1, SDF1 = 29.2, sDF2 = 36.7, gCF = 46.9, gDF1 = 18.6, gDF2 = 18.2, gDFP = 16.3) (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by concordance factor analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: High-quality mammalian genomes can be obtained from roadkill samples using MaSuRCA hybrid assembly combining Illumina short reads and Nanopore long reads.
source: By relying on this protocol, we were able to generate two hybrid assemblies by combining Illumina reads at relatively high coverage (50-60x) and MinION long reads at relatively moderate coverage (11-13x), which provided genomes with high contiguity and completeness.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by the assembly statistics and quality metrics presented in Table 1 and comparison with other carnivoran genomes.

claim: The hybrid assemblies are of better quality than all the draft genome assemblies generated using the DISCOVAR de novo protocol based on a PCR-free single Illumina 250 bp paired-end library used in the 200 Mammals Project of the Broad Genome Institute.
source: The benefit of adding Nanopore long reads is demonstrated by the fact that our hybrid assemblies are of better quality than all the draft genome assemblies generated using the DISCOVAR de novo protocol based on a PCR-free single Illumina 250 bp paired-end library (Weisenfeld et al., 2014) used in the 200 Mammals Project of the Broad Genome Institute (Zoonomia Consortium, 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by comparison with other genome assemblies, with citations to Weisenfeld et al., 2014 and Zoonomia Consortium, 2020.

claim: The earliest available name for the East African aardwolf subspecies is P. c. septentrionalis (Rothschild, 1902).
source: The earliest available name for the East African aardwolf subspecies is P. c. septentrionalis (Rothschild, 1902).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Rothschild, 1902.

claim: P. c. septentrionalis was first distinguished based on pelage characteristics of a specimen from Somaliland, which has a creamy white pelage without any gray tinge, but washed slightly with buff in the neck and side of the rump.
source: This subspecies was first distinguished based on pelage characteristics of a specimen from Somaliland, which has a creamy white pelage without any gray tinge, but washed slightly with buff in the neck and side of the rump (Rothschild, 1902).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Rothschild, 1902.

claim: The Southern aardwolf subspecies P. c. cristatus was described as ashy gray, front and sides of neck grayish white, black stripes broad and well defined.
source: In contrast, the Southern aardwolf subspecies P. c. cristatus was described as ashy gray, front and sides of neck grayish white, black stripes broad and well defined (Rothschild, 1902).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Rothschild, 1902.

claim: Postorbital breadth is significantly greater in P. c. septentrionalis than P. c. cristatus.
source: Adding in measurements of skulls from the literature (Allen et al., 1909; Heller, 1913; Hollister, 1924; Roberts, 1951; Roberts, 1932) confirmed that postorbital breadth is significantly greater in P. c. septentrionalis than P. c. cristatus but revealed no significant differences between other skull measurements including condylobasal length of skull (Appendix 2—figure 2, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by morphometric analysis shown in Appendix 2—figure 2 and Supplementary file 7, with citations to multiple literature sources.

claim: The global long-term Plio-Pleistocene African climate is still debated.
source: However, the global long-term Plio-Pleistocene African climate is still debated.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and reflects current scientific uncertainty.

claim: Some studies have suggested an evolution toward increased aridity in Eastern Africa during the Plio-Pleistocene.
source: For Eastern Africa, some studies have suggested an evolution toward increased aridity (deMenocal, 2004; deMenocal, 1995)
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to deMenocal, 2004 and deMenocal, 1995.

claim: Other studies have proposed the opposite trend (toward wetter conditions) for Eastern Africa during the Plio-Pleistocene.
source: For Eastern Africa, some studies have suggested an evolution toward increased aridity (deMenocal, 2004; deMenocal, 1995), whereas others have proposed the opposite (Grant et al., 2017; Maslin et al., 2014; Trauth et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Grant et al., 2017; Maslin et al., 2014; and Trauth et al., 2009.

claim: The 30–10 kya period appears to have been more humid in Southern Africa.
source: Finally, the 30–10 kya period appears to have been more humid (Chase et al., 2019; Chevalier and Chase, 2015; Lim et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Chase et al., 2019; Chevalier and Chase, 2015; and Lim et al., 2016.

claim: The global decrease in population size detected in the Southern and Eastern populations could reflect the fragmentation of a continuous ancestral range.
source: The global decrease in population size detected in the Southern and Eastern populations could also reflect the fragmentation of a continuous ancestral range.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents a speculative interpretation of the PSMC results.

claim: The global trend toward a wetter climate may have favored the development of the tropical rainforest in central Africa, creating a belt of unsuitable habitat.
source: The global trend toward a wetter climate may have favored the development of the tropical rainforest in central Africa, creating a belt of unsuitable habitat.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents a speculative interpretation of the demographic results.

claim: Several bird species have similar disjunct distributions as the aardwolf and bat-eared fox, including the Orange River francolin (Scleroptila gutturalis), the greater kestrel (Falco rupicoloides), the double-banded courser (Smutsornis africanus), the red-fronted tinkerbird (Pogoniulus pusillus), the Cape crow (Corvus capensis), and the black-faced waxbill (Estrilda erythronotos).
source: Interestingly, several bird species also have similar distributions including the Orange River francolin (Scleroptila gutturalis), the greater kestrel (Falco rupicoloides), the double-banded courser (Smutsornis africanus), the red-fronted tinkerbird (Pogoniulus pusillus), the Cape crow (Corvus capensis), and the black-faced waxbill (Estrilda erythronotos), supporting the role of the environment in the appearance of these disjunct distributions.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents knowledge about biogeographic patterns.

claim: The monophyly of all superfamilies within Carnivora is strongly supported.
source: Across the Carnivora the monophyly of all superfamilies are strongly supported (Flynn et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by phylogenomic analysis and a citation to Flynn et al., 2010.

claim: One third of the nodes (three out of nine) within the Felidae show controversial node supports.
source: There is one interesting point regarding the Felidae. While almost all the nodes of the phylogeny were recovered as strongly supported from the three phylogenetic inference analyses (ML inferences, concordance factor analyses and coalescent-based inferences), one third of the nodes (three out of nine) within the Felidae show controversial node supports.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The controversial node supports within the Felidae are consistent with previous studies arguing for ancient hybridization among the Felidae.
source: This result is not surprising and is consistent with previous studies arguing for ancient hybridization among the Felidae (Li et al., 2019; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Li et al., 2019 and Li et al., 2016.

claim: The difficulty of resolving the trifurcation among the Arctoidea subfamilies has likely been contradictory due to incomplete lineage sorting (ILS).
source: Considering these results, the difficulty of resolving this trifurcation among the Carnivora (Delisle and Strobeck, 2005) has likely been contradictory due to the ILS observed among these three subfamilies (Doronina et al., 2015), which led to different phylogenetic scenarios depending on methods (Peng et al., 2007) or markers (Yu and Zhang, 2006) used.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to multiple studies on ILS and phylogenetic methods.

claim: At the genomic level, the Mephitidae is the sister-group to all other Musteloidea families.
source: In that sense, despite incomplete lineage sorting (Doronina et al., 2015), at the genomic level, it seems that the Mephitidae is the sister-group to all other Musteloidea families.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 5, with a citation to Doronina et al., 2015.

claim: The protocol developed to extract DNA from roadkill samples increased the median size of the sequenced raw DNA fragments threefold in the case of aardwolf.
source: This protocol increased the median size of the sequenced raw DNA fragments threefold in the case of aardwolf (Tilak et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Tilak et al., 2020.

claim: Using the high accuracy option rather than the fast option of Guppy 3.1.5 leads to more contiguous assemblies by increasing the N50 value.
source: In line with previous studies (Wenger et al., 2019; Wick et al., 2019), we found that using the high accuracy option rather than the fast option of Guppy 3.1.5 leads to more contiguous assemblies by increasing the N50 value.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Wenger et al., 2019 and Wick et al., 2019.

claim: The carnivoran hybrid assemblies are fairly comparable to those obtained using the classic Illumina-based genome sequencing protocol involving the sequencing of both paired-end and mate-paired libraries.
source: Overall, our carnivoran hybrid assemblies are fairly comparable to those obtained using the classic Illumina-based genome sequencing protocol involving the sequencing of both paired-end and mate-paired libraries (Li et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by comparison with other genome assemblies, with a citation to Li et al., 2010.

claim: The two hybrid assemblies could form the basis for future chromosome-length assemblies by adding complementary HiC data.
source: Moreover, these two hybrid assemblies could form the basis for future chromosome-length assemblies by adding complementary HiC data (van Berkum et al., 2010) as proposed in initiatives such as the Vertebrate Genome Project (Koepfli et al., 2015) and the DNA Zoo (Dudchenko et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to van Berkum et al., 2010; Koepfli et al., 2015; and Dudchenko et al., 2017.

claim: The cost of producing each of the Carnivora genomes was 5,000–10,000 USD.
source: Our results demonstrate the feasibility of producing high-quality mammalian genome assemblies at moderate cost (5,000–10,000 USD for each of our Carnivora genomes) using roadkill
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents data on the cost of genome sequencing.

claim: The subspecies of O. megalotis fall into the 'gray zone' of the speciation continuum and are likely undergoing incipient speciation due to their vicariant distributions.
source: The subspecies of O. megalotis fall into the 'gray zone' of the speciation continuum (De Queiroz, 2007; Roux et al., 2016) and are likely undergoing incipient speciation due to their vicariant distributions.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to De Queiroz, 2007 and Roux et al., 2016, representing an inference from the genetic data.

claim: Natural hybridization has been reported between C. aureus and C. lupus.
source: Despite known cases of natural hybridization reported between C. aureus and C. lupus (Galov et al., 2015; Gopalakrishnan et al., 2018), the taxonomic rank of these two species is well accepted.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Galov et al., 2015 and Gopalakrishnan et al., 2018.

claim: The taxonomic rank of C. aureus and C. lupus as separate species is well accepted.
source: Despite known cases of natural hybridization reported between C. aureus and C. lupus (Galov et al., 2015; Gopalakrishnan et al., 2018), the taxonomic rank of these two species is well accepted.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents established taxonomic knowledge.

claim: The ML phylogenetic tree inferred from the mitogenomic dataset was robust, with 91.4% of the nodes (128 out of 140) recovered with bootstrap support higher than 95%.
source: Maximum likelihood (ML) analyses reconstructed a robust mitogenomic phylogeny, with 91.4% of the nodes (128 out of 140) recovered with bootstrap support higher than 95% (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The COX1 dataset includes 3,657 sequences for 150 species of Carnivora.
source: These datasets include 3,657 COX1 sequences for 150 species and 6,159 CYTB sequences for 203 species of Carnivora
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents data on the mitochondrial barcoding datasets.

claim: The CYTB dataset includes 6,159 sequences for 203 species of Carnivora.
source: These datasets include 3,657 COX1 sequences for 150 species and 6,159 CYTB sequences for 203 species of Carnivora
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents data on the mitochondrial barcoding datasets.

claim: The mitogenomic phylogeny recovered the clade Ailuridae/Mephitidae as a sister clade to all other Musteloidea families.
source: Interestingly, our phylogenetic reconstruction based on mitogenomic data recovered the clade Ailuridae/Mephitidae as a sister clade to all other Musteloidea families.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by mitogenomic phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The phylogenomic inferences based on the genome-scale supermatrix recovered the Mephitidae as the most basal family of the Musteloidea.
source: The phylogenomic inferences based on the genome-scale supermatrix recovered the Mephitidae as the most basal family of the Musteloidea. This result is supported by both coalescent-based inferences and concordance factors.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Aardwolves and bat-eared foxes live in open environments including short-grass plains, shrubland, and open and tree savannas.
source: Aardwolves and bat-eared foxes live in open environments including short-grass plains, shrubland, and open and tree savannas, and both are highly dependent on herbivorous termites for their diet.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents established ecological knowledge.

claim: Both aardwolves and bat-eared foxes are highly dependent on herbivorous termites for their diet.
source: Aardwolves and bat-eared foxes live in open environments including short-grass plains, shrubland, and open and tree savannas, and both are highly dependent on herbivorous termites for their diet.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents established ecological knowledge.

claim: The median number of single-copy orthologues recovered for each species was 12,062 out of the 14,509 single-copy orthologues extracted from the OrthoMaM database.
source: Then, single-copy orthologous gene identification resulted in a median of 12,062 out of the 14,509 single-copy orthologues extracted from the OrthoMaM database for each species
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by orthologous gene identification analysis.

claim: The new hybrid assemblies allowed the recovery of 12,062 genes for the Southern aardwolf (P. c. cristatus).
source: Our new hybrid assemblies allowed the recovery of 12,062 genes for the Southern aardwolf (P. c. cristatus), 12,050 for the Eastern aardwolf (P. c. septentrionalis), and 11,981 for the Southern bat-eared fox (O. m. megalotis) (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by gene annotation data in Table 1.

claim: The new hybrid assemblies allowed the recovery of 12,050 genes for the Eastern aardwolf (P. c. septentrionalis).
